paper.central_claim: An agent-based active exploration framework (planning, perception and execution modules with fine-grained perception-execution interleaving, built on OpenClaw) lets a robot find initially invisible, distractor-surrounded targets and complete a real-world Find-and-Place task, improving robustness and adaptability over passive execution; reported success 95.7% without and 94.3% with distractors.
paper.title: From Passive Execution to Active Exploration: Agentic Embodied Manipulation in Realistic Environments

signatures.object: A planner (OpenClaw agent; underlying LLM unnamed) coordinating a local perception module and a local execution (skill) module over atomic operation units; baseline implied: passive predefined plans, not run.
signatures.information: User instruction, the current visual observation, the interaction history; perception returns recognised objects, localisation, OCR text and scene state; the target is hidden at the start.
signatures.operation: Planner selects the next exploratory or manipulative unit (search region, inspect cue, open drawer, retrieve, place); execution performs one atomic operation; perception re-observes and reports visibility/progress; planner decides whether to continue, close, or move on.
signatures.output: A sequence of skill invocations on a Franka arm.
signatures.conditions: Two category-labelled multi-drawer cabinets on a table; one target category (pear toy) in three variants; lemon-shaped distractors.
signatures.feedback: Perception outputs after every atomic operation.
signatures.selection_rule: None beyond the planner's judgement; no gate or verifier is described.
signatures.later_use: n/a: static agent design, no retained-improvement claim
signatures.failure_boundary: Failure categories are named but no counts, latency, planner identity, skills or perception models are reported.

gap.author_gap: Most embodied manipulation frameworks follow a passive execution paradigm that assumes visible, uncluttered targets; real settings have occlusion, distractors and semantic cues.
gap.checked_gap: Plausible and widely recognised, but not evidenced: no failing passive baseline is run and nearest planning-based methods are dismissed in one sentence by citation number.
gap.closest_adjacent: Unspecified: cited neighbours are described only as 'carefully engineered modules and less generalizable paradigms'.
gap.residue: Active search under partial observability with category-label cues in a real cabinet scene.
gap.stakes: Gap between laboratory-style and real deployment settings.
gap.method_response: Closed-loop planner/perception/execution with perception re-run after every atomic operation.
gap.remaining_gap: Everything quantitative: baselines, ablations, trial counts, failure analysis, the LLM and skills used, cost.
unresolved: Whether prior planning-based methods fail on this task is untested.

claims.text: The framework completes the real-world Find-and-Place task with about 95% success.
claims.setting: Franka arm; two cabinets with labels; pear-toy target in three variants; with and without lemon distractors.
claims.result: 95.7% (no distractor) and 94.3% (distractor); per-variant 94.0-96.0%; trial counts not given.
counterevidence: No denominators, judge, or failure breakdown.
claims.allowed_conclusion: The authors report roughly 95% success on one real task; counts are unverifiable.

claims.text: Active exploration and fine-grained interleaving improve robustness over passive execution.
claims.result: Only the proposed system's rates are shown.
counterevidence: No passive baseline, no interleaving ablation.

claims.text: The system generalises beyond a single fixed visual instance.
claims.setting: Three appearance variants of a single pear target category.
claims.result: Success differs by at most 1-2 points across variants.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Narrow appearance robustness for one category is reported.

claims.text: The system is practical on consumer hardware.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Local perception/execution fits one consumer GPU; planner cost unknown.

assessment.evidence_level_note: Closed-loop real-robot success rates are reported but without per-task trial counts, a baseline or a stated success judge, so the EVIDENCE 'online' bar (counts per task) is not met; graded offline pending counts.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: The authors report that a planner/perception/execution agent on a real Franka arm completed a hidden-object Find-and-Place task at about 94-96% success across three variants of one object; the number of trials, the success judge and any comparison with passive execution are not reported, so the improvement claims are unsupported.

evidence.quote: we propose an agent-based active exploration framework that enables robots to dynamically interact with the environment rather than merely execute predefined instructions.
evidence.support_explanation: Central framework claim.

evidence.quote: Specifically, our framework consists of three collaborative modules: a planning module for high-level task reasoning, a perception module for visual scene understanding, and an execution module for low-level manipulation.
evidence.support_explanation: Three-module decomposition.

evidence.quote: Instead of executing a complete action sequence based on the initial observation, the robot invokes the execution module for one atomic operation and calls the perception module to update its understanding of the environment.
evidence.support_explanation: Interleaving operation: one atomic operation then re-perception.

evidence.quote: The overall system is built upon OpenClaw, which serves as the agentic framework and planning module for high-level task reasoning.
evidence.support_explanation: Planner is OpenClaw; the underlying LLM is not named.

evidence.quote: The perception and execution modules are implemented locally.
evidence.support_explanation: Perception/execution models and skills are not specified.

evidence.quote: We deploy the proposed framework on a Franka robotic arm in the real world.
evidence.support_explanation: Real-robot deployment, one arm.

evidence.quote: The target object is placed inside an unknown drawer and is not visible from the initial observation.
evidence.support_explanation: Task: hidden target, two cabinets with category labels.

evidence.quote: A trial is considered successful only if the robot correctly identifies the relevant cabinet, searches the drawers until the target object is found, grasps the target object, and places it into the box.
evidence.support_explanation: Success definition; who judges it is not stated.

evidence.quote: Failure cases include selecting the wrong cabinet, stopping before finding the target, grasping a distractor, or failing to complete the final placement.
evidence.support_explanation: Failure categories are defined but no breakdown is reported.

evidence.quote: we evaluate one representative setting where the pear toy is specified as the target object.
evidence.support_explanation: Evaluation covers one target category.

evidence.quote: Target Object Variant 1 96.0 94.0 Target Object Variant 2 96.0 95.0 Target Object Variant 3 95.0 94.0 Overall 95.7 94.3
evidence.support_explanation: Results table without trial counts or baselines.

evidence.quote: Even with visually similar distractors, the success rate only slightly decreases from 95.7% to 94.3%, demonstrating that the proposed active exploration strategy can robustly identify, search for, and manipulate the intended target in cluttered and ambiguous environments.
evidence.support_explanation: Author interpretation of the single result table.

evidence.quote: However, most existing embodied manipulation frameworks still follow a largely passive execution paradigm.
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap statement.

evidence.quote: While some planning-based methods [ 1 , 3 , 4 , 7 ] have considered such scenarios, they often rely on carefully engineered modules and less generalizable paradigms.
evidence.support_explanation: Nearest neighbours are named only by citation number and are not compared.

evidence.quote: The entire system can run on a consumer-grade NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU
evidence.support_explanation: Only hardware cost information.

evidence.quote: We further introduce a perception–action interleaving strategy, which updates scene understanding after each fine-grained operation to support more reliable long-horizon execution.
evidence.support_explanation: Second claimed contribution, with no ablation.

evidence.quote: It extracts task-relevant information through object recognition, target localization, optical character recognition (OCR), and scene-level semantic understanding.
evidence.support_explanation: Perception outputs by role only.

evidence.quote: we decompose a long-horizon manipulation task into fine-grained operation units, such as opening a drawer, closing a drawer, and picking up an object.
evidence.support_explanation: Semantic action vocabulary executed by a skill module.

evidence.quote: The results show that our framework achieves consistently high success rates across all target-object variants, indicating strong generalization beyond a single fixed visual instance.
evidence.support_explanation: Generalisation claim from three toy variants of one object category.

evidence.quote: Experimental results demonstrate that our framework improves the robustness and adaptability of embodied manipulation in challenging scenarios
evidence.support_explanation: Improvement claim; no comparison condition exists.

evidence.quote: Depending on the task progress, the planner may decide to search a specific region, inspect a semantic cue, open a container, retrieve an object, or place the object at a target location.
evidence.support_explanation: Planner decision space.

evidence.quote: Given a planned subtask, it converts the high-level decision into executable robot actions and drives the robot to interact with the environment.
evidence.support_explanation: Execution module role only.

evidence.quote: Each cabinet is associated with a different object category and marked with a category label on its top surface.
evidence.support_explanation: Setup detail: category labels make the cabinet inferable by OCR.

evidence.quote: In addition, we introduce visually similar lemon-shaped distractors to evaluate the system’s robustness under visual ambiguity.
evidence.support_explanation: Distractor variant.

G.reason: A familiar, plausible gap (passive execution) with no quantification, no named failing baseline and neighbours dismissed by citation number; remaining gap boundary is unspecified.

M.reason: Re-perceiving after every atomic operation is a sensible mechanism for hidden-object search and a concrete example is given, but the explanation is generic and there is no distinguishing prediction against a coarse-perception alternative.

X.reason: Module roles and the plan-act-perceive cycle are described, but the planner LLM, perception models, skills, prompts, hand-back or failure handling are not specified; conditions and failure boundaries are absent.

E.measurement.reason: A success definition is given, but denominators, the success judge, and a baseline are missing; the rate table cannot be tied to counts.

E.causality.reason: No baseline, ablation of interleaving or modules, or alternative-explanation test exists in the full text.
